table.title: AI Recommendations_Early vs Late_Authencity Mediation
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
H1: Participants will perceive a person as less creative and exerting less effort when AI recommendations are used at the beginning of the development of an idea, compared to when the AI recommendations are used at the end.
H2: Participants will perceive the person integrating AI recommendations early (as compared to late) in the idea development process as being less authentic in their work process, and consequently will perceive the person to be less creative (as compared to late).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Perceived creativity: How would you rate the level of creativity in Jordan's approach to music production?
Perceived effort: How much effort do you think Jordon has put into producing the song? 1(not at all creative) - 7(very creatrive)

To measure perceived authenticity in the work process, we will ask two questions, and we will average them to create an index for the measure.
Q.1. How authentic do you think Jordon's approach was in designing the song? 1(not at all) - 7(very much so)
Q.2. To what extent do you think Jordon was genuine in his work process? 1(not at all) - 7(very much so)
table.study_design_overview: Two conditions in the between-subjects design: using AI recommendations at the beginning of the idea development vs using AI recommendations at the end of the idea development.
table.statistical_tests:
1. We will conduct three separate independent samples t-tests using the condition: using AI recommendations (at the beginning vs at the end) of the creative process as the independent variable and the mean estimate of perceived creativity, effort, and perceived authenticity in the work process as the dependent variables.
2. We will conduct a mediation analysis  (Model 4 of the PROCESS macro for SPSS with 10,000 bootstraps; Hayes, 2013) with the timing of AI integration (beginning vs end) as the independent variable, perceived authenticity in the work process as the mediator, and perceived creativity as the dependent variable.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants who answer "Yes" to the question "Have you ever been on the planet Jupiter?" will be excluded from analyses. We will only analyze complete responses.
table.sample_size: 300 U.S. American Participants will be recruited from the Connect Cloud Research platform before exclusion.
table.additional_comments:
We will also collect data for the mediator perceived alienation using three items, which we will average to create an index:
1. To what extent do you feel that engaging with creations in the music industry offers lasting value?
2. To what extent do you feel that engaging with creations in the music industry has a meaningful impact on you?
3. To what extent do you feel you have control over the creations in the music industry?
Participants will answer all three questions on a scale of 1(not at all) - 7(very much so).

We will conduct a mediation analysis  (Model 4 of the PROCESS macro for SPSS with 10,000 bootstraps; Hayes, 2013) with the timing of AI integration (beginning vs end) as the independent variable, perceived authenticity in the work process and perceived alienation as parallel mediators, and perceived creativity as the dependent variable.

table.title: AI Recommendations_Early vs Late_Authencity and Autonomy Manipulation
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
H1: Participants will perceive the creator as less creative and exerting less effort when AI recommendations are used at the beginning of the development of an
idea, compared to when the AI recommendations are used at the end.

H2: The extent of using AI recommendations (directly implementing the recommendations exactly as suggested by the AI vs. modifying them before implementing) may moderate this perceived creativity and effort.

H3a: When the creator incorporates AI recommendations at the beginning of the development process (compared to at the end), participants are likely to perceive the creator as having less autonomy in how they wish to work. Consequently, participants will perceive the creator as less creative in their work (as compared to when AI is integrated in the end).

H3b: Participants will perceive the person integrating AI recommendations at the beginning (as compared to the end) of the idea development process as being less authentic in their work process, and consequently will perceive the person to be less creative (as compared to the end).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Perceived creativity: How would you rate the level of creativity in Alex's approach to designing the new line of designer shirts? 1(not at all creative) - 7(very creatrive)
Perceived effort: How much effort do you think Alex has put into designing this new line of designer shirts? 1(not at all) - 7(very much)

Two mediators in parallel: perceived autonomy of the creator in the work process and perceived authenticity of the creator in the work process

To measure the perceived autonomy of the creator in the work process, we will ask two questions and average them to create an index for the measure.
Q.1. To what extent do you think Alex was free to design the new line of shirts in the way that he wanted? 1(not at all) - 7(very much so)
Q.2. To what extent do you think Alex maintained control over the process of designing the new line of shirts? 1(not at all) - 7(very much so)

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "We report Welch's t-tests when Levene's test was significant (p < .05) and Tukey or Bonferroni corrections for pairwise comparisons."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. text.text: Does the timing of artificial intelligence (AI) integration into creative work affect how creators are judged?

While analysis of more than 70,000 creative requests to ChatGPT found that creators often integrate AI early, four main and eight supplemental experiments (N = 5,272) revealed that creators are perceived as less creative when they integrate AI recommendations early rather than late in their creative work.
This occurs partly because creators are perceived as less effortful and less authentic when they integrate AI recommendations early.
This penalty generalizes across creative domains, persists even when the total AI contribution is held constant, and holds regardless of the creator's expertise.
Communicating that the creator modified rather than directly implemented AI recommendations attenuates the penalty.

Moving beyond existing research comparing judgments of whether creators use AI versus do not, our research demonstrates that when and how creators integrate AI into the creative process also shape judgments.
Imagine Jordan and Alex presenting advertising campaigns created using artificial intelligence (AI) tools.
Jordan used AI early in the creative process, while Alex used AI late in the process.
If both creators contributed an equal amount of creative input, would they be judged differently simply because they integrated AI early or late into their creative process?

This is important to consider because creative work often requires creators to bring in other individuals and tools to advance ideas toward implementation (Boussioux et al., 2024; Mahaney et al., 2025).

text.text: Research on the timing of AI use has primarily focused on what creators produce, finding that independent ideation before AI integration boosts creators' originality and confidence (Qin et al., 2025).

text.text: However, how people judge creators based on when AI entered their work remains unclear.

Because people seldom observe creative processes directly and may instead infer the creator's contribution from observable cues, when AI enters the creative process can be such a cue that leads to biased evaluations.

text.text: Accordingly, neither the early nor the late parts of the creative workflow should be treated as proxies for distinct creative modes or explicit differences in the type of creative work performed.
Because the creative process can change iteratively during a creator's workflow, the temporal dimension becomes a relevant manipulation (Tolkamp et al., 2025).

text.text: However, it is unclear whether people perceive creators differently based on when they integrate AI into their creative process.

The decision of when to integrate AI tools can be understood through the lens of entrainment, where the pacing and rhythm of processes are influenced by temporally structured events (Ancona et al., 2001; Omidvar et al., 2025).

text.text: Actors therein interpret temporal cues and respond with actions, such as synchronizing with external constraints or deciding when to integrate help to deliver a creative product (Fisher et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Actors therein interpret temporal cues and respond with actions, such as synchronizing with external constraints or deciding when to integrate help to deliver a creative product <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Fisher et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Within these temporally bound cycles, creators can decide to integrate AI tools, such as during the early or late phases of their creative work.
Importantly, then, choosing when to integrate AI reflects the creator's strategic choice rather than necessarily a creative deficiency (Zhou & Lee, 2024).
text.formatted: Importantly, then, choosing when to integrate AI reflects the creator's strategic choice rather than necessarily a creative deficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Zhou & Lee, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Successful creative outcomes rely on both the creator's skill and AI's capability (Huang, 2025).
text.formatted: Successful creative outcomes rely on both the creator's skill and AI's capability <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Huang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although the consequences of AI tool integration may vary across creative tasks and workflows, it is unclear whether evaluators respond differently depending on whether it enters early or late in the creative process.
Nevertheless, people and decision-makers rarely observe creative processes directly.
They infer from observable cues (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992; Gilbert & Malone, 1995), such as when AI entered the workflow, without considering why the creator did so.
text.formatted: They infer from observable cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gilbert & Malone, 1995)</ref>, such as when AI entered the workflow, without considering why the creator did so.

text.text: Consequently, the timing of AI integration can cue assessments of the creator's creativity, regardless of their actual intent.
The directional effect of the timing of AI integration on perceived creativity, whether early or late AI integration is penalized more, is not obvious.

Early AI integration might be perceived as strategic and efficient, reserving human cognition for high-value judgments later in the work (Jia et al., 2024), while late AI integration might signal underutilization of AI's potential.
text.formatted: Early AI integration might be perceived as strategic and efficient, reserving human cognition for high-value judgments later in the work <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Jia et al., 2024)</ref>, while late AI integration might signal underutilization of AI's potential.

text.text: Further, research on the 'late action effect' shows that actions closer to outcomes are seen as more causally influential because of heightened counterfactual thinking and reversibility (Ziano & Pandelaere, 2022).
text.formatted: Further, research on the 'late action effect' shows that actions closer to outcomes are seen as more causally influential because of heightened counterfactual thinking and reversibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Ziano & Pandelaere, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, receiving help late in a task undermines well-being as compared to early help (Koo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Relatedly, receiving help late in a task undermines well-being as compared to early help <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Koo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Peak-end effects research also shows that people disproportionately judge the overall agency, authorship, and impact of a sequence based on the endpoints rather than the initial efforts (Alaybek et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Peak-end effects research also shows that people disproportionately judge the overall agency, authorship, and impact of a sequence based on the endpoints rather than the initial efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alaybek et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, AI integration at the end of a creative process may increase both evaluator scrutiny of the creator's independent role and doubts about human creative contribution, leading to less favorable reactions than AI integration early in the process.
Although an increased penalty for late AI integration is plausible, we propose that early AI integration reduces perceived creativity more than late integration does.

That is, while integrating AI in creative work generally faces a penalty in the evaluator's perceptions (Benegal et al., 2026; Reif et al., 2025; Schilke & Reimann, 2025), we suggest the penalty is higher when a creator integrates AI early rather than late in their creative work.
text.formatted: That is, while integrating AI in creative work generally faces a penalty in the evaluator's perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Benegal et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Reif et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Schilke & Reimann, 2025)</ref>, we suggest the penalty is higher when a creator integrates AI early rather than late in their creative work.

text.text: Because people tend to attribute creativity and original thinking more to humans than to AI tools (Horton Jr et al., 2023), AI's position in the temporal sequence of work might shape evaluators' judgments.
text.formatted: Because people tend to attribute creativity and original thinking more to humans than to AI tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Horton Jr et al., 2023</ref>), AI's position in the temporal sequence of work might shape evaluators' judgments.

text.text: When AI is integrated early, evaluators may infer that the creator relied on algorithmic assistance to accomplish the part of the work that typically signals originality (Epstein et al., 2023; Friedman, 2008).
text.formatted: When AI is integrated early, evaluators may infer that the creator relied on algorithmic assistance to accomplish the part of the work that typically signals originality <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Epstein et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Friedman, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, integrating AI later can preserve the creator's originality because the AI assists with work the creator has already developed.
As a result, evaluators may be less likely to discount the creator's creativity.
Therefore, we hypothesize: H1: Creators are perceived as less creative when they integrate AI recommendations early rather than late in their creative work.
We do not assume that timing changes who de facto owns the creative work, who is responsible for the final product, or the total contribution.
Instead, we examine whether similar general assistance from an AI tool receives different evaluations depending on whether it enters the creative workflow earlier or later.
We further suggest that early AI integration reduces perceived creativity more than late integration does because it also diminishes perceived effort and authenticity to a greater extent.
We theorize that perceived effort and authenticity operate in parallel.

We propose that the early AI integration penalty in creativity judgments partially stems from creators being perceived as exerting less effort when using AI earlier than later in their creative process.
Effort has traditionally been a crucial metric for assessing individuals, which prompts people to publicly signal effort (Inzlicht et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Effort has traditionally been a crucial metric for assessing individuals, which prompts people to publicly signal effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Inzlicht et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: People often use effort as a heuristic in judgments of quality and value (Kruger et al., 2004; Norton et al., 2012).
text.formatted: People often use effort as a heuristic in judgments of quality and value <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Kruger et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Norton et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Generally, using AI might not be seen as effortful because AI assistance in work is generally seen as effort-saving (Bechwati & Xia, 2003), reducing time on tasks (Fieldhouse, 2025), which can increase concerns that creators might become overly reliant on AI tools (Lira et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Generally, using AI might not be seen as effortful because AI assistance in work is generally seen as effort-saving <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bechwati & Xia, 2003)</ref>, reducing time on tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fieldhouse, 2025)</ref>, which can increase concerns that creators might become overly reliant on AI tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Lira et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Taking AI assistance also creates ambiguity regarding how much credit belongs to the creator versus the help they received (Kay et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Taking AI assistance also creates ambiguity regarding how much credit belongs to the creator versus the help they received <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kay et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, creators may be expected to invest more time and effort early rather than late in their process.
Early AI integration may signal that the creator is taking a shortcut in the phase where effort is presumed to matter most because it was used before creator involvement was substantially observable.
In contrast, late AI integration gives evaluators more opportunities to infer that a creator engaged substantially in the creative task before receiving assistance from an AI tool.
Indeed, individuals using AI are perceived as lazier and less capable than those who use non-AI technologies (Reif et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, individuals using AI are perceived as lazier and less capable than those who use non-AI technologies <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Reif et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The inference of effort here is precisely regarding the amount of creator involvement that is visible before any external tools are integrated.

Since effort has traditionally been the standard for assessing output (Buell & Norton, 2011; Fuchs et al., 2015; Garcia-Rada et al., 2022; Kruger et al., 2004), and evaluators value work that carries visible human labor (Inzlicht et al., 2018; Judge et al., 2020), reduced perceived effort in early versus late AI integration may result in diminished creativity judgments.
text.formatted: Since effort has traditionally been the standard for assessing output <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Buell & Norton, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Fuchs et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Garcia-Rada et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Kruger et al., 2004)</ref>, and evaluators value work that carries visible human labor <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Inzlicht et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Judge et al., 2020)</ref>, reduced perceived effort in early versus late AI integration may result in diminished creativity judgments.

text.text: Therefore, we hypothesize that: H2: Perceived effort mediates the effect of AI integration timing on perceived creativity.

We further propose that the early AI integration penalty also stems from reduced perceptions of authenticity: Creators who integrate AI early in the process are seen as less authentic than those who use it later, and reduced authenticity reduces perceptions of creativity.
Authenticity involves expressing ideas originating from oneself and acting consistently with one's unique identity (Amabile & Pratt, 2016; Goncalo & Katz, 2020).

text.text: Authenticity assessment relies on how well the outcome truly reflects the creator's vision, and technological interventions that might be seen as corrupting (Moulard et al., 2014; Sun & Pham, 2025).

text.text: Conversely, taking credit for creative work that is not one's own reduces perceived authenticity (Ellis, 2022), presumably because the greater the creator's creative control over their work, the more authentic they are perceived to be (Valsesia et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Conversely, taking credit for creative work that is not one's own reduces perceived authenticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ellis, 2022)</ref>, presumably because the greater the creator's creative control over their work, the more authentic they are perceived to be <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Valsesia et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Generally, using AI tools in creative work may raise authenticity concerns.
For instance, AI-designed fashion products and marketing communications are seen as less authentic than human-created ones (Kirk & Givi, 2025; Lee & Kim, 2024).

text.text: Building on this logic, we theorize that the timing of AI integration can serve as a salient cue for evaluating perceived authenticity.
Early integration of AI may signal that the creator failed to exert creative control, and the resulting outcome reflects AI outputs more than the creator's authentic voice.

Conversely, in late AI integration, the creator maintains more creative control over the process, and the outcome may align more closely with their vision, thereby preserving the perceived authenticity more effectively.

Since authenticity is emblematic of genuine individual perspectives and personal essence (Cheng et al., 2008) it prompts the impression of originality, which is a marker of creative merit (Nunes et al., 2021).

text.text: Early integration of AI tools may therefore lead evaluators to view the creator's engagement with the work as less personal expression.
On the other hand, late AI integration may make the creator's prior engagement and expression more visible, supporting stronger inferences that the creator was genuinely involved.
Therefore, we hypothesize that: H3: Perceived authenticity mediates the effect of AI integration timing on perceived creativity.

text.text: Theoretical Model
Field data from more than 70,000 creative requests to ChatGPT suggest that most creators use AI earlier, rather than later, in the creative work.

Yet across four main and eight supplementary experiments (all preregistered; total N = 5,272; including U.S. American, British, and French participants), this research reveals a robust temporal asymmetry in how creators' creativity in AI-assisted work is evaluated.
Study 1 demonstrates that creators who integrate AI late are perceived as more creative than those who integrate early.
Study 2A reveals that decreased perceived effort and authenticity mediate the negative effect of early AI integration on creativity judgments.
Study 2B finds that emphasizing that the creator elaborated on AI suggestions rather than directly implementing them significantly attenuated the early AI integration penalty.
Finally, Study 3 revealed that managers allocate higher bonuses and are more likely to implement and recommend outcomes from late AI integrators.

In supplementary studies, we rule out expertise of the creator as a boundary condition for the early AI integration penalty (Study S1), find that the penalty is not reduced when AI is framed as trained on the creator's own style (Study S2) and that it is stronger for hand-sculpted than for 3D-printed work (Study S3), generalize the effect across six professional contexts (Study S4A) and to a French sample (Study S4B), replicate it in a different artistic context with a marketplace consequence (Study S4C), replicate the moderating role of usage beliefs (Study S5), and extend the effect from AI to human assistance (Study S6).

text.text: We operationalized AI integration timing in two ways.

In Studies 1, 2A, 2B, and 3 (and Studies S1, S4A, S4C, and S5), we specified whether the AI recommendations supported activities early (e.g., generating initial sketches) or late (e.g., finalizing design layouts) in the creative process.
Because these descriptions vary in both the AI's contribution and the timing of its use, Studies S2, S3, S4B, and S6 provide a conservative test.
In these studies, the AI recommendations were used only during the first 25% or the last 25% of the task, and no activities were described.
Timing was therefore the only feature that differed between the early-AI and late-AI conditions, and the penalty held in these studies as well (meta-analytic g = -0.40; see Supplementary Material).

Before examining how evaluators judge the timing of AI integration, we examined when creators actually integrate AI into their creative work.

We analyzed WildChat-4.8M (W. Zhao et al., 2024), a public corpus of ChatGPT conversations that users consented to share, collected between April 2023 and July 2025 across models from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o and o1.

text.text: Of 1,658,803 English conversations, we identified creative requests from keywords in the opening message (full keyword lists in the Supplementary Material).
A broad filter identified 801,629 conversations that opened with a creative request (e.g., a story, poem, song, slogan, design, or marketing content).

Within these, we flagged two overlapping subsets: requests in the creative domains that informed our experimental scenarios (fashion, music, advertising and marketing, product development, research proposals, public communication, training, and sculpture and art), and requests in professional contexts with organizational stakes (advertising, marketing, branding, product development, innovation, communication, training, and research proposals).

We then coded each request's timing as "early-AI" if it asked the AI to produce the work (e.g., "write a," "create a," "come up with") and as "late-AI" if it asked the AI to work on the creator's existing draft (e.g., "improve," "proofread," "here is my draft").
Requests matching neither or both patterns were left uncoded.
Because some prompts were submitted thousands of times, often by automated bots, we counted each distinct request once and estimated 95% confidence intervals by resampling users.
Of 70,451 coded requests from 31,233 users, 85.9% (95% CI [84.6, 87.4]) integrated AI early, roughly six for every request that brought AI in late (see Figure 2).

text.text: Early-AI requests also predominated in the creative domains that informed our experimental scenarios later (84.5%, 95% CI [83.2, 85.8]) and in professional contexts (71.5%, 95% CI [69.8, 73.2]).

The early AI integration pattern held for one request per user (85.6% early AI); when requests matching both keyword lists were included in the analysis, regardless of whether all were counted as late-AI (78.0%) or early-AI (87.2%).

The pattern also held across all ChatGPT models (72.5% to 89.2%), in each year from 2023 to 2025, among requests of similar length (84.7%), and in a multilevel model controlling for user, country, message length, model, and year (87.7%; Supplementary Material).
Few early-AI conversations asked the AI to revise its output (1.1%).

The study used a between-subjects design with three conditions: early-AI, late-AI, and control (no timing information).

Participants in the "early-AI" condition read the following scenario: "Alex Chen is a fashion designer at a premium clothing brand.
He has extensive experience designing clothing lines.
While developing a new line of designer shirts, Alex decided to integrate recommendations from an AI-powered tool at the beginning of the fashion development process.
Alex used the AI's recommendations to generate initial sketches, propose different color palettes, and suggest different fabric patterns."
Participants in the "late-AI" condition read the following scenario: "Alex Chen is a fashion designer at a premium clothing brand.
He has extensive experience designing clothing lines.
While developing a new line of designer shirts, Alex decided to integrate recommendations from an AI-powered tool at the end of the fashion development process.
Alex used the AI's recommendations to finalize the design layouts, refine the color effects, and optimize the fabric specifications."

In the "no timing" condition, participants read that Alex integrated recommendations from an AI-powered tool into the fashion development process, but the text provided no timing information or details about the nature of the AI's use.

Next, participants rated Alex's creativity ("How would you rate the level of creativity in Alex's approach to fashion designing?") on a 7-point scale anchored at 1 (not at all creative) and 7 (very creative).

Importantly, if early AI integration is common in real-world creator workflows, this finding suggests that most creative AI use falls into the category evaluators penalize most.
Having established this basic effect, we next examine why it occurs.

text.text: We predict that integrating AI early rather than late in the creative process leads to lower perceived effort and authenticity, which, in turn, is associated with lower creativity judgments.

After applying the pre-registered exclusion criteria (300 recruited, 0 excluded), the sample included complete responses from 300 U.S. American participants recruited through the Connect Cloud Research platform (148 males, 150 females, 2 preferred not to disclose gender; Mage = 40.55, SD = 9.10).
This study had a between-subjects design with two conditions: early-AI or late-AI.
This sample size allows us to detect effect sizes of Cohen's d = 0.32 or larger with 80% power and 5% alpha (two-tailed) in independent-samples t-tests.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the between-subjects conditions.
Participants in the "early-AI" condition read the following scenario: "Jordan Parker is a hip-hop producer in the recording industry.
He has extensive experience producing songs in a broad range of musical styles.
While working on a new single for an album, Jordan decided to integrate recommendations from an AIpowered music tool at the beginning of the music production process.
He utilized the AI's recommendations to help him generate ideas for a novel rhythm and produce a unique beat for the song."
Participants in the "late-AI" condition read the following scenario: "Jordan Parker is a hip-hop producer in the recording industry.
He has extensive experience producing songs in a broad range of musical styles.
While working on a new single for an album, Jordan decided to integrate recommendations from an AIpowered music tool at the end of the music production process.
He utilized the AI's recommendations to help him finalize the song, polish the rhythm, and tighten up the beat."

Following this, participants rated Jordan's creativity ("How would you rate the level of creativity in Jordan's approach to music production?") on a 7-point scale anchored at 1 (not at all creative) and 7 (very creative).
To measure perceived effort, participants responded to "How much effort do you think Jordan has put into producing the song?"
on a 7-point scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much).
To measure perceived authenticity, participants completed two items: "How authentic do you think Jordan's approach was in designing the song?"
and "To what extent do you think Jordan was genuine in his work process", both on 7point scales from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much so).
These items were averaged to create an authenticity index (Cronbach's α = .967).

This study uncovers two key explanations of the effect of AI integration timing on creativity judgment: perceived effort and authenticity.
When creators integrate AI early in their work rather than late, evaluators perceive them as both less effortful and less authentic, leading to lower creativity ratings.
Next, we examine whether our proposed mechanism, through perceived effort and authenticity, has process-consistent evidence.

This study revealed that informing evaluators that the creator elaborated on AI recommendations attenuated the early integration of AI penalties related to perceived creativity, effort, and authenticity.

This indicates that when evaluators learn that creators elaborated on AI suggestions as part of their creative process, it diminishes the timing effect by restoring perceptions of effort and authenticity.
We next examine whether the penalty carries over to managers' consequential decisions.

Moving beyond evaluators' reactions, this preregistered study (https://aspredicted.org/2qjp-9vsk.pdf) investigates whether professional managers differ in decisions about bonus allocation, project execution, and recommendations to higher management for employees who integrate AI early versus late in their workflows.

text.text: Specifically, we predict that early AI integration would be perceived as less creative and elicit less favorable managerial reactions than late AI integration.

After applying the pre-registered exclusion criteria (301 recruited, 0 excluded), the sample included complete responses from 301 U.S. American managers recruited through the Connect Cloud Research platform's panel of verified managers (148 males, 152 females, 1 preferred not to disclose gender; Mage = 39.86, SD = 9.08).

The sample included 32% in senior management roles, 28% as assistants or associates, 17% as C-suite executives or directors, 16% as analysts, and 7% as consultants across fields such as marketing, product management, and customer experience.
The study used a between-subjects design with two conditions: early-AI or late-AI.
This sample size allows us to detect effect sizes of Cohen's d = 0.32 and larger with 80% power and 5% alpha (two-tailed) for pairwise comparisons.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subjects conditions.
Participants were asked to imagine themselves as a senior marketing manager at an audio technology firm.
Next, they learned that their company had partnered with an advertising agency tasked with delivering a campaign for its new line of headphones.
As managers, they are responsible for managing the campaign's development and helping guide strategic decisions for this advertising work.
Following this, participants were presented with a scenario describing Sarah Martinez, the advertising agency's creative director.
In the early-AI condition, participants read the following scenario: "Sarah Martinez is the creative director at the advertising agency.
She has extensive experience developing advertising campaigns.
While developing the campaign, Sarah decided to integrate recommendations from an AI-powered tool at the beginning of the advertising campaign development process.
She utilized the AI's recommendations to help her generate campaign message concepts, illustrate mood boards, and uncover customer insights."
Participants in the late-AI condition read the following scenario: "Sarah Martinez is the creative director at the advertising agency.
She has extensive experience developing advertising campaigns.
While developing a new campaign for an upcoming product, she uses AI-powered design tools at the end of the advertising campaign development process.
She utilized the AI's recommendations to help her polish the campaign messaging, finalize advertising layout, and optimize audience targeting parameters."

Next, to measure perceived creativity and effort, participants provided their opinions on the questions "As a marketing manager responsible for the advertising campaign, how would you rate the level of creativity in Sarah's approach to advertising campaign development?"
and "How much effort do you think Sarah has put into designing this advertising campaign?"
on a scale of 1(not at all creative/not at all) to 7(very creative/very much).

Following this, participants made three responses intended to mimic typical workplace decisions: (1) willingness to implement the campaign without changes by responding to the question "As a marketing manager responsible for the advertising campaign, how willing would you be to implement Sarah's advertising campaign without any further changes?"

on a scale of 1(not at all) to 7(very much), (2) likelihood of recommending the campaign to senior leadership by responding to the question "As a marketing manager responsible for the advertising campaign, how likely are you to recommend that your company's senior leadership implement Sarah's advertising campaign without any changes?"
on a scale of 1(not at all likely) to 7(very likely), and (3) bonus allocation.

For the bonus allocation measure, participants were informed that their company allocated a discretionary bonus pool ($12,500) based on creative work, which amounts to 5% of the total campaign budget of $250,000.
Next, participants reported, in an open-ended response, the amount in USD they would be willing to allocate to Sarah based on their assessment of Sarah's creative work.

Error bars reflect 95% confidence intervals.

This study revealed that professional managers not only perceive creators who integrate AI early as less creative than those who integrate it late, but also translate these perceptions into tangible penalties: lower bonuses, a lower likelihood of project implementation, and a lower likelihood of project recommendations to upper management.
These suggest that disclosure of when AI is used could significantly influence career outcomes in creative industries.

Across 12 preregistered experiments (total N = 5,272), we demonstrate a robust temporal asymmetry: creators are perceived as less creative when they integrate AI early rather than late in their creative process (meta-analytic effect size, g = -0.61, 95% CI [-0.73, -0.49]).

This early AI integration penalty generalized across several creative domains (Studies 1, 2A, 2B, S4A, and S4C), held when AI assistance was confined to an equal share of the work (Studies S2, S3, S4B, and S6), and did not depend on the creator's expertise (Study S1) or on whether the AI was trained on the creator's own data (Study S2).
Mediation evidence suggested that parallel reductions in perceived effort and perceived authenticity partly explained it (Studies 2A and 2B).
The penalty was attenuated when evaluators learned that the creator elaborated on, rather than directly implemented, the AI recommendations (Studies 2B and S5).

text.text: Contrary to our prediction, the early-AI integration penalty was attenuated when the work was 3D-printed rather than hand-sculpted (Study S3).

text.text: Finally, people were willing to pay less for products made with early AI integration (Study 2B), and managers gave early AI integrators smaller bonuses and were less willing to implement or recommend their work (Study 3).

After applying the pre-registered exclusion criteria (400 recruited, 0 excluded), the sample included complete responses from 400 U.S. American participants recruited through the Connect Cloud Research platform (201 males, 196 females, 2 other, 1 preferred not to disclose gender; Mage = 38.19, SD = 9.77).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions in a 3 (usage: control vs. direct implementation vs. elaborate and modify) × 2 (timing: early-AI vs. late-AI) full factorial between-subjects design.
This sample size allows us to detect effect sizes of Cohen's f = 0.16 or larger for the interaction between usage and timing with 80% power and a 5% alpha (two-tailed).
All participants read about Alex Chen, a fashion designer at a premium clothing brand with extensive experience designing clothing lines and developing a new line of designer shirts.
We manipulated the timing of AI integration by stating, "Alex decided to integrate recommendations from an AI-powered tool at the beginning (end) of the fashion development process."
This was similar to the manipulations we used in Study 1.

Importantly, to highlight the nature of usage of AI suggestions by the creator, participants in the "direct implementation" condition read, "Alex reviewed the AI's recommendations and directly implemented them, using them exactly as they were suggested by the AI".
While participants in the "elaborate and modify" condition read, "Alex reviewed the AI's recommendations and elaborated on them, modifying them from how they were suggested by the AI".
Following this, participants rated perceived creativity, effort, and authenticity (two items: Cronbach's α = .959) using the same measures as in Study 2A.

As an exploratory measure, we assessed a downstream consequence by asking participants to report, in an open-ended response, the amount in U.S. dollars they would be willing to pay for a designer shirt made by Alex.

This research makes three theoretical contributions.
First, we identify the timing of AI integration as a consequential dimension of AI disclosure in creative work.

Prior research (Benegal et al., 2026; Kirk & Givi, 2025; Raj et al., 2026; Reif et al., 2025; Schilke & Reimann, 2025) has primarily examined the consequences of AI disclosure on workplace trust, social evaluations, and perceptions of AI-assisted products and outputs.

text.text: We extend this literature by shifting the unit of analysis from output to creators and from whether AI was used to when it was used.

Moreover, withholding timing information appears to offer little protection because evaluators who learned only that AI was used rated the creator closer to the early-AI than to the late-AI creator (Study 1).
This "guilty until proven innocent" pattern suggests that creators who remain silent about the timing of AI integration may face a penalty similar to that of creators who disclose early integration.
Second, we identify two parallel process inferences: perceived effort and perceived authenticity.

The findings extend research on creativity heuristics like visible effort (Buell & Norton, 2011; Kruger et al., 2004) and creative control (Valsesia et al., 2016) by demonstrating that the timing of AI integration shifts both perceptions simultaneously.

text.text: People tend to see creative work as an expression of the self (Goncalo & Katz, 2020).

text.text: AI assistance used early therefore may diminish perceptions of authenticity at the very stage where such personal imprint is expected to emerge.

The same two pathways emerged when early assistance came from a human colleague rather than AI (Study S6), suggesting that the penalty may reflect lay beliefs about where creativity resides, not just concerns specific to AI.

Third, we contribute to research on human-AI collaboration (Arora et al. 2025; Huang 2025) by identifying a key boundary condition: evaluators respond less negatively to early AI integration when the creator's role is described as elaborating on and modifying the AI recommendations rather than implementing them directly.

text.text: Our findings suggest that they also shape how creators are judged.
Our findings also offer several practical implications.
First, strategically disclosing when an AI tool is used can immunize creators from credibility erosion.
Creators who use AI at the end of the creative process benefit from transparent disclosure, as evaluators reward late integration with higher creativity attributions.
When integration occurs early, emphasizing that the creator adapted and modified AI recommendations rather than implementing them directly may attenuate the early-integration penalty (Study 2B).
Notably, framing AI as trained on one's own creative style does not provide similar protection (Study S2), suggesting creators should focus disclosure on active modification of AI output.

Second, because field evidence suggests most creators use AI early, organizations should recognize that current evaluation practices may systematically disadvantage employees who openly disclose early AI use.

In Study 3, managers gave smaller bonuses, were less willing to implement the campaign, and were less likely to recommend it to senior leadership when the creator disclosed early rather than late AI integration.
Consequently, employees may hide beneficial AI usage to avoid evaluation penalties, reducing sharing and organizational learning about effective human-AI workflows.

Organizations may reduce this penalty by separating evaluation of the final output and its impact from interpretive assumptions about when AI help was used, and by establishing norms that treat early AI integration as a strategic choice rather than a signal of low creativity.
Third, product marketing can leverage timing cues to preserve perceived value.
When accurate, product descriptions and marketing campaigns could describe AI as an "assistant" used late in the process, highlighting the creator's initial effort and authentic vision.
Marketing communications that restore perceptions of effort and authenticity could also mitigate penalties associated with AI disclosure.
Several limitations of our research offer directions for future research.
First, our studies used single-creator scenarios, although many creative endeavors involve teams (Kay et al., 2018).
text.formatted: First, our studies used single-creator scenarios, although many creative endeavors involve teams <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kay et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The timing of AI integration and its effects on evaluations of team creativity remain unexplored.
While we expect the temporal asymmetry to hold, the effect's intensity may vary by team composition and other factors.

Second, because we compared AI integration at the early and late stages of the creative process, whether integration in the middle, or at several points, is judged more like early or late integration remains open for future research (Acharya et al., 2025).

text.text: Third, our samples consisted of participants based in the US, UK, and France.
Given the variations in how creativity is conceptualized across cultures (Leung & Morris, 2011), the early integration penalty might vary across cultures.
text.formatted: Given the variations in how creativity is conceptualized across cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Leung & Morris, 2011)</ref>, the early integration penalty might vary across cultures.

text.text: Cultures higher in individualism might penalize early AI integration more severely than cultures higher in collectivism.
Fourth, while we identified effort and authenticity as parallel explanations, other psychological processes likely contribute as well.
Perceived autonomy (Breaugh, 1985) may matter, such that early AI integration could signal reduced self-determination over creative direction.

text.text: Future research should examine other candidate mechanisms, potentially with alternative mediators included simultaneously.
Fifth, our scenarios explicitly describe timing information, which may increase attention to this cue beyond naturalistic settings.
Nonetheless, as AI disclosure becomes common through transparency norms, platform watermarking, or regulation, timing information will become more accessible.
Future research should examine how effects manifest when timing must be inferred.
